hints: Look closely at point X at about 0.18 s, where is the dashed left ventricle line compared to the dotted left atrium line just before and just after X?
Remember blood always pushes from high pressure to low pressure, so what must happen to the valve between atrium and ventricle when ventricular pressure first rises just above atrial pressure?
walkthrough:
**Spot what is happening at X**

Look at time about 0.2 s. Just before X, the left atrium (dotted line) is slightly above the left ventricle (dashed line). This is atrial systole pushing blood into the ventricle.

At X, the dashed ventricle line crosses and rises sharply above the dotted atrium line. That tells you ventricular systole is starting.

**Apply the valve pressure rule**

Valves are simple pressure gates. They open when pressure behind them is higher, and they are forced shut when pressure in front of them is higher to stop backflow.

Here the rule is:
$$ \text{if ventricular pressure > atrial pressure, AV valve closes} $$

**Link to the cardiac cycle**

As soon as left ventricular pressure exceeds left atrial pressure at X, blood would tend to flow back into the atrium. The atrioventricular (bicuspid) valve slams shut to prevent this.

This marks the start of ventricular systole and produces the first heart sound. So X is AV valve closure.

options.A: Correct. At X ventricular pressure first exceeds atrial pressure, so the atrioventricular valve is pushed shut to prevent backflow into the atrium.
options.B: Not correct. AV valves open when atrial pressure is greater than ventricular pressure, which happens earlier during filling and later at about 0.5 s, not at X where the ventricle becomes higher.
options.C: Not correct. Semilunar valves close when aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure at the end of ventricular systole, around 0.45 s on the graph, not at X.
options.D: Not correct. Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, which happens a little after X at about 0.2 s when the dashed line rises to meet the solid aorta line.
